statement: In eight men given MDMA 75 mg and 125 mg on separate days in a randomized, double-blind crossover, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.81 times higher (236.4 against 130.9 ug/L) and a 24-hour exposure 1.97 times higher (2623.7 against 1331.5 ug x h/L), so blood levels rose more than the dose did (de la Torre et al., 2000; ratios from the printed means). Clearance outside the kidneys fell from 74.0 to 38.1 L/h while clearance by the kidneys did not change, and across the five dose levels from 50 to 150 mg, with different men at each level and only two men at each of the lowest and highest, the 24-hour exposure ranged from 100.1 to 5232.0 ug x h/L, so differences between men are mixed in with the dose. The authors give two explanations, saturation of MDMA's breakdown (which they say cannot be excluded) and MDMA's blocking of the enzyme CYP2D6 that breaks it down, and state that the observations were retrospective and the studies were not designed to detect this. The authors' abstract goes further, concluding that this holds for the whole population whatever the CYP2D6 genotype and that small increases in the amount taken give disproportionate rises in blood level, so that people are more prone to acute toxicity; the dose comparison was made in men with normal CYP2D6 only and no toxicity outcome was measured. In a later study of 15 men, one dose of MDMA switched CYP2D6 off, and the enzyme's activity had not fully recovered after 10 days (O'Mathuna et al., 2008); this fits the second explanation, as does the small difference between people with and without a working enzyme (Schmid et al., 2016). The authors of the 2008 study infer, without giving a second dose, that a second dose taken up to a week later would give higher concentrations and, they add, a higher risk of acute toxicity. People can feel little from an amount for several reasons (a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts the effect, bodies that differ) and some take more. None of these studies tested people who took more because they felt little: the amounts were fixed and given to healthy men in a laboratory, and what they show is that a larger single amount gave a larger rise in blood level than the amount itself. Second doses taken 2 or 24 hours after a first are covered in the library's separate claim on acute tolerance.
plain: A bigger amount of MDMA gave more in the blood than the extra amount alone would explain. In 8 men, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak level 1.8 times higher and about twice the total exposure over the day. MDMA seems to switch off the liver enzyme that clears it, so more MDMA is cleared more slowly (the authors' explanation, not proven). The authors also say that small increases in the amount could raise blood levels out of proportion and so make acute toxicity more likely; the study did not measure toxicity. Some people feel little from an amount and take more, for reasons such as a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that mutes the effect, or bodies that differ. These studies did not test that: they gave fixed amounts to healthy men in a lab. What they show is that a larger amount gave a larger rise than the amount itself. Second doses are covered in the answer on tolerance.
population: Healthy adult men with earlier MDMA experience in laboratory studies: 14 men (8 in a randomized crossover at 75 and 125 mg; 6 in a pilot at 50, 100 and 150 mg) and, for the mechanism, 15 men in a probe-drug study
exposure: A larger single dose of MDMA (study conditions: 75 mg and 125 mg, and 50, 100 and 150 mg in the pilot, by mouth)
comparator: The same eight men at the smaller dose, with dose-normalized exposure as the yardstick
outcome: Peak and 24-hour exposure of MDMA in plasma, dose-normalized exposure, kidney and non-kidney clearance, and recovery of urinary MDMA and HMMA
magnitude: 75 mg against 125 mg, 8 men (de la Torre et al., 2000): peak 130.9 (SD 38.6) against 236.4 (58.0) ug/L; AUC(0-24 h) 1331.5 (646.0) against 2623.7 (572.9) ug x h/L; dose-normalized AUC 17.8 (8.6) against 21.0 (4.6), paired t test of AUC(0-infinity) P<0.03, 90% interval of the within-person ratio -0.3 to 89.3%; non-renal clearance 74.0 against 38.1 L/h (P<0.03); total clearance 86.9 (74.4) against 51.1 (14.1) L/h as printed; unchanged MDMA in urine 71.2 (13.7) against 169.6 (69.5) micromol. Across 50 to 150 mg, 24-hour exposure 100.1 and 813.9 (two men at 50 mg) against 5132.8 and 5232.0 (two men at 150 mg); Kruskal-Wallis test of dose-normalized exposure P<0.1. Editors' calculation from the printed means: 1.67 times the dose gave 1.81 times the peak and 1.97 times the exposure.

evidence.locator: Methods > Patients and study design, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Abstract (Methods)
evidence.extracted: Fourteen men took part: six in a pilot phase (two each at 50, 100 and 150 mg) and eight in a double-blind, randomized, Latin-square crossover of 75 mg MDMA, 125 mg MDMA, 40 mg amphetamine and placebo; all had used MDMA at least five times; in the second phase all were extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers. The 150 mg volunteers had side effects that ruled out higher doses, and 50 mg was judged low.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (image; MDMA rows for 75 and 125 mg); Results, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: In the same eight men, 125 mg gave a higher dose-normalized exposure than 75 mg: peak 236.4 ug/L (SD 58.0) against 130.9 (38.6); AUC(0-24 h) 2623.7 (572.9) against 1331.5 (646.0); dose-normalized AUC 21.0 (4.6) against 17.8 (8.6); half-life 8.6 (3.2) against 7.7 (3.2) h. A paired t test of dose-normalized AUC(0-infinity) gave P<0.03, and the 90% interval of the within-person ratio was -0.3 to 89.3%, so the authors judged the 125 mg dose not bioequivalent to the 75 mg dose scaled by dose. Editors' calculation: 1.67 times the dose gave 1.81 times the peak and 1.97 times the AUC.

Urinary clearance of MDMA was roughly constant across doses (analysis of variance not significant) while non-renal clearance depended on dose (P<0.03) and, in the same eight men, was about halved at 125 mg (38.1 L/h) against 75 mg (74.0 L/h), which the authors read as impaired hepatic clearance; total clearance was 86.9 (SD 74.4) against 51.1 (14.1) L/h. The SDs of non-renal clearance are cut off at the edge of the table image.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (image; 50, 100 and 150 mg rows); Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Across the five doses (50 to 150 mg, a 3-fold range), with different men at each dose, the AUC(0-24 h) of MDMA ranged from 100.1 to 5232.0 ug.h/L (more than 10-fold): two men at 50 mg had 100.1 and 813.9 ug.h/L, two men at 150 mg 5132.8 and 5232.0, with peak concentrations 441.9 and 486.9 ug/L at 150 mg against a mean of 236.4 at 125 mg. A Kruskal-Wallis test of dose-normalized AUC(0-infinity) across the five doses was only marginal (P<0.1).

The authors name two explanations: saturation of MDMA metabolism (the simplest, which they say cannot be excluded) and inhibition of CYP2D6-mediated demethylenation by MDMA, and perhaps by its metabolite HMMA, citing in vitro work showing MDMA is both a substrate and an inhibitor of CYP2D6. Their stated limits: the observations were made retrospectively, the clinical studies were not designed to detect the phenomenon, and bias cannot be excluded because the same individuals were not tested at each dose level.

The abstract concludes that the lack of proportionality, in a window of doses the authors call compatible with recreational use, is a more general phenomenon concerning the whole population independent of CYP2D6 genotype, and that relatively small increases in the dose ingested give disproportionate rises in plasma concentration, so that people are more prone to acute toxicity. Editors' reading: the dose comparison was made in eight men who were all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers, so independence from genotype was not tested, and no toxicity outcome was measured.
evidence.quote: subjects are more prone to develop acute toxicity

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 527); Results › Plasma Concentrations of DEX, DOR, MM, HM, and MDMA Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamic Effects, 1st paragraph (p. 528); Results › Urinary DEX/DOR MR and CYP2D6 Recovery Half-Life, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 528)
evidence.extracted: In 15 men, a single MDMA dose of 1.5 mg/kg raised the exposure to the CYP2D6 probe drug dextromethorphan from 15.7 to 149.1 (area over 8 hours) and its peak from 3.5 to 29.7 ng/mL, lowered the product dextrorphan from 464.6 to 31.9 ng/mL at peak, and raised the urinary probe-drug to product ratio from 0.0061 to 0.4322; the recovery half-life was 46.6 hours (SD 11.8) on one fit, and the ratio had not fully recovered at 10 days.

The authors recall their own earlier study in which MDMA concentrations were increased beyond what accumulation predicts when a second dose was taken 24 hours later. They also write that people who use MDMA are known to take on average more than 1 pill per session (1.8 to 2.9 pills on average, up to 6 to 7 depending on the type of person, citing their reference 36, which was not read) and that many binge for several days, and infer, without having given a second dose, that a second dose taken up to a week later would give higher plasma concentrations and, they add, a higher risk of acute toxicity. No second dose, concentration-effect measure or toxicity outcome was studied here (editors' reading).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 'Taken together' paragraph (also the following paragraph on limitations)
evidence.extracted: The authors read the small and short-lived difference between people with and without CYP2D6 function as the result of MDMA inhibiting CYP2D6 itself, citing a physiologically based model that estimates a rise of only 36% in peak MDMA with no CYP2D6 function; they note that other enzymes and CYP3A4 inhibition may matter more than CYP2D6 genetics.

evidence.locator: MDMA pharmacology and metabolic disposition, 4th paragraph; Drug-drug interactions, 1st paragraph; Concluding remarks, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Narrative review, second-hand. MDMA is both a substrate of CYP2D6 (O-demethylenation to HHMA, then methylation to HMMA) and a potent mechanism-based inhibitor; the review gives metabolic clearance as about 75% of MDMA plasma clearance, with about 30% of its metabolism regulated by CYP2D6 (citing the 2000 non-linear paper and a 2005 paroxetine-probe study), written elsewhere as less than 30% and, for both drugs, lower than 50%.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 overall high on the study card, set by an unplanned retrospective analysis, the dependence of the wider dose range on two men per dose, statistical inconsistencies and a table misprint. One level, not two, because the 75 against 125 mg comparison is randomized and within-person and the concentrations are objective.

inconsistency.note: No contrary result in the studies read here; the editor should weigh the library's claim on acute tolerance, where a booster study reports a peak ratio close to the dose ratio.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for the doses and men studied and does not extend to other doses, women or settings.

imprecision.note: Eight men; the 90% interval of the within-person ratio reaches zero; the 50 to 150 mg range rests on two men per dose.

grade.reasoning: The 75 against 125 mg comparison is a randomized, double-blind, within-person crossover and starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -2 (eight men, an interval reaching zero, two men per dose in the wider range) give very low. Status single-study: one study shows the dose comparison; the probe-drug and genotype studies bear on the mechanism, not on dose proportionality. The claim describes the blood levels in fixed-dose laboratory conditions; it is not guidance on any amount.

verification.flag_note: Second-dose studies (Farre 2004, Peiro 2013, Humbert-Droz 2026) are anchored in the library's claim on acute tolerance, not here, and were not read for this claim; the editor may join the two claims. Note for the editor: that claim's booster study reports a peak ratio of 1.50 for a total dose ratio of 1.5, close to proportional, which may bear on inconsistency. Printed Table 2 value 40.9 in de la Torre et al. (2000) is probably 4.9 (see its card). The Table 1 and Table 2 values were read from the table images on the PMC page and were not checked a second time; the text confirms the 125 mg peak, the halved non-renal clearance and the more-than-10-fold range, and the dose-normalised AUCs reproduce from the AUCs and doses.
